result.summary: Ulysses, disguised as a beggar, fights and crushes the tramp Irus, then warns the suitor Amphinomus of coming doom. Penelope, made radiant by Minerva, draws gifts from the suitors, and Ulysses is mocked by Melantho and Eurymachus, who hurls a stool at him before Telemachus ends the evening.

scenes.title: Ulysses fights Irus
scenes.summary: Irus insults Ulysses, the suitors set them to fight, and Ulysses knocks Irus down with a measured blow and drags him out.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks exposing his identity if he shows too much strength; Irus risks a beating and mutilation.

scenes.title: Warning to Amphinomus
scenes.summary: Amphinomus greets Ulysses kindly, and Ulysses warns him to leave before the master returns. Amphinomus is troubled but doomed.
scenes.stakes: Amphinomus's life, as Minerva has doomed him to die by Telemachus's hand.

scenes.title: Penelope made beautiful
scenes.summary: Minerva inspires Penelope to appear before the suitors, puts her to sleep and beautifies her. Penelope rebukes Telemachus over the stranger's treatment.
scenes.stakes: Penelope risks being forced into an unwanted marriage; Telemachus faces his mother's reproach.

scenes.title: Penelope collects gifts
scenes.summary: Eurymachus praises Penelope, who recalls Ulysses' parting words and reproaches the suitors' ways. They bring gifts and she withdraws; the suitors dance until dark.
scenes.stakes: Penelope faces a forced remarriage once Telemachus is grown.

scenes.title: Braziers and the stool
scenes.summary: Ulysses tends the lights and faces taunts from Melantho and Eurymachus, who throws a stool that hits the cupbearer. Telemachus sends the suitors home.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks injury and exposure while enduring insults.

characters.name: Ulysses
characters.description: disguised king of Ithaca, posing as a beggar

alias_notes.explanation: His birth name; the young men nicknamed him Irus because he ran errands.

notable_quotes.reason: Ulysses' reflection on human vanity and fortune's changeability.
Ulysses' veiled threat of his return and the suitors' coming slaughter.

analysis.text: Hospitality and its abuse: the suitors mistreat a beggar, while Amphinomus's kindness is noted but cannot save him.
Disguise and restraint: Ulysses holds back his strength and temper to prepare his vengeance.

legacy.text: The Irus fight made 'Irus' a byword for a poor beggar in later European literature.

fun_facts.text: Irus's nickname comes from Iris, the gods' messenger, because he ran errands.

language_notes.text: Irus recalls Iris, the gods' messenger; the nickname mocks him for running errands. The footnote number 148 is an editor's marker, not part of the story.
"Giving me the wink" means signalling secretly; the suitors are quietly encouraging Irus to throw Ulysses out.
A "fish-fag" is a fishwife, a coarse woman selling fish; Irus compares Ulysses' chatter to her scolding.
"Paunches" are stomachs of animals; stuffed with blood and fat they were cooked like sausages, a prized dish.
"To throw them off the scent" means to mislead them; Ulysses pretends to be weak and hungry so no one suspects his strength.
Echetus is a cruel king of the mainland, mentioned elsewhere in the poem as a byword for savagery.
"Achaeans" is Homer's general name for the Greeks; here it means the suitors and others in the hall.
"Importunity" means persistent, annoying demands; the suitors mean Irus's constant begging.
"Pledging him" means drinking his health, a gesture of friendly greeting, here done by raising the goblet to the beggar.
"Vouchsafes" means graciously grants or allows.
"Part bloodlessly" means they will not separate without bloodshed; Ulysses is hinting at the coming slaughter while still disguised.
"Foreboded" means had a presentiment of, felt in advance that something bad would happen.
"Heaven robbed me of all my beauty": Penelope says her grief since Ulysses sailed for Troy has ruined her looks, so she refuses to wash and anoint herself.
"Cloister" here means the colonnaded hall or porch of the house where the suitors gather, not a religious building.
"Ambrosial" means divine, belonging to the gods; ambrosia was their food and cosmetic, conferring immortality and radiance.
Diana (the Greek Artemis) was believed to bring gentle sudden death to women, so Penelope asks her for a painless end.
"Staid" means sober and respectable, so the maids lend Penelope's appearance before the men a proper dignity.
Iasian Argos is probably the Peloponnese or Greece generally; Achaeans is a general name for the Greeks. Eurymachus means all Greece would send suitors.
"We shall not all of us come safe home" means some of the Greek warriors will die at Troy.
Ulysses tells her to remarry once their son Telemachus has a beard, meaning once he is grown to manhood.
Penelope refers to the custom that suitors bring gifts and feasts to the woman's family, rather than consuming her household's goods.
Braziers are metal stands or baskets holding burning wood, used for light and warmth in the hall.
"Gibe" means to mock or jeer at someone with scornful remarks.
A smithy and a place of public gossips were where idle men gathered; she tells him to sleep there like a vagrant.
"Cudgel" means to beat with a short heavy club.
"Wolds" are open upland country; here, farmland away from the town where a hired laborer would work.
The doors' narrowness is a threat: when Ulysses returns, the suitors will be fleeing and unable to escape through them.
Clasping someone's knees was the formal gesture of a suppliant seeking protection.
Drink-offerings (libations) of wine were poured to the gods at the end of a meal before guests departed.

context_notes.text: Beggars depended on the hospitality of wealthy houses. Irus is a rival for the suitors' scraps, which is why he resents Ulysses, who is disguised as a beggar.
Telemachus, Ulysses' son, speaks as host, though he has little real power over the suitors; he does not yet know the beggar is his father.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is Ulysses' protector and often alters his appearance and strength to help him.
Dulichium is an island near Ithaca. Amphinomus is one of the suitors who came from there, and he is portrayed as more decent than the others.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) is Ulysses' patron goddess and supports his revenge, so she has already marked this suitor for death despite his decency.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) protects Ulysses' household and works to prepare Penelope and the suitors for the coming revenge.
Venus (the Greek Aphrodite) is the goddess of love and beauty; the Graces are her attendant goddesses of charm and grace.
Irus is the beggar who was set to fight the disguised Ulysses for the suitors' amusement and was beaten.
Ulysses is present in the hall disguised as a beggar, so he secretly watches his wife's behaviour.
Eurydamas, Pisander and Antinous are among the leading suitors, each competing to outdo the others in gifts.
Melantho is one of Penelope's maids and sister of the goatherd Melanthius; her disloyalty contrasts with the care Penelope gave her.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) protects Ulysses and here deliberately stokes the suitors' insolence to justify their coming punishment.
Amphinomus is the most decent of the suitors, which is why Ulysses turns to him for protection.

literary_notes.text: Ulysses says Irus will not come to "the house of Ulysses" again, speaking of himself in the third person while the audience knows his identity.
Teeth knocked out "like boar's tusks" is a vivid, brutal comparison showing Irus's bluster.
The suitors marvel at the strength under the rags, unaware they are seeing the true master of the house and their own doom.
The suitors "nearly died of laughter" exaggerates their callous amusement, which contrasts with the bloody violence and foreshadows their fate.
The suitors repeat Antinous's threat against Irus, mocking him cruelly, while they themselves are soon to be slain by the beggar they praise.
Ulysses states a general truth about human changeability, that gods give men their moods day by day, to teach humility.
Ulysses, disguised as a beggar, speaks of his own return as a future event. Amphinomus does not realize he is addressing the man he fears.
The narrator announces Amphinomus' death at Telemachus' hand, so his kindness and worried walk away gain tragic weight.
Penelope's remark that the suitors "speak fairly" but "mean mischief" is a sharp, truthful judgment disguised as a pretext for her appearance.
Penelope's radiance is compared to Venus's own and to ivory, elevating her beauty to divine, precious perfection.
Penelope laments her misery while the reader knows her husband is present in the hall, disguised as the beggar.
Telemachus's contemptuous picture of the beaten Irus shows his growing confidence and his open hostility toward the suitors.
Penelope's dread of a coming night of forced marriage raises tension about the approaching contest and Ulysses' revenge.
The suitors take Penelope's flattery at face value, while Ulysses, unknown to them, understands her real purpose and approves.
The chain's amber beads are compared to sunlight, emphasising the gift's brilliance and value.
Ulysses brooding on things that "should surely come to pass" hints at the coming slaughter of the suitors.
Eurymachus's joke about the light from the beggar's bald head mocks the very man whose return will bring the suitors destruction.
Living in "a little world, and that a bad one" figuratively condemns Eurymachus's narrow, corrupt outlook.
Eurymachus repeats Melantho's insults almost word for word, showing the household's shared contempt and echoing her taunt.
